main_damage_causes: Reassignment of Seamus's active comic agency in the Nearly Headless Nick scene to Ron and Hermione, removing his most distinct characterization moment in the book corpus.
Loss of small but telling peer-interaction beats (Harry putting out Seamus's fire, the communal laughter at his family anecdote) that established his ease and warmth within the Gryffindor group.

Seamus functions in the film primarily as a running visual gag (repeated explosions) rather than as a voiced, curious, socially active character, reducing him from a distinct personality to a one-note background comic device.

Seamus's irreverent, sardonic comic voice is systematically reduced: the film retains his laugh at Lockhart but strips the follow-up lines and physical comedy beats that define his personality in the book corpus.

The one scene where the film gives Seamus a speaking line in a dramatic moment (Common Room, scene 108) replaces his characteristic wit with a generic anxious-student reaction, misrepresenting his book characterisation.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 – Sorting feast / Nearly Headless Nick introduction
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, it is sandy-haired Seamus Finnigan who interrupts Sir Nicholas's preferred formal introduction ('I would prefer you to call me Sir Nicholas de Mimsy--') and who asks 'Nearly Headless? How can you be nearly headless?' and later 'How did he get covered in blood?' – Seamus drives the comic interrogation of Nick and is an active, curious voice at the feast.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film, Ron identifies Nick and Hermione asks 'Nearly headless? How can you be nearly headless?' Seamus's only contribution is a brief self-introduction about his half-and-half parentage. His role as the curious, interruptive questioner of Nick is entirely absorbed by Ron and Hermione.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Seamus loses two distinct book moments of comic agency and personality at the feast – his cheeky interruption of Nick and his morbid curiosity about the blood. These small beats establish him as an inquisitive, irreverent presence. Reassigning them to Ron and Hermione erases his voice in this scene.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 – Moving staircases / portraits corridor
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book corpus does not place Seamus in this precise corridor scene, but the film gives Neville the line 'Seamus, that picture's moving!' which at least names him as present and reacting. No unfaithful distortion of his characterization occurs here.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Seamus is merely named by Neville as a bystander. This is neutral – no characterization is given or taken away.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minimal damage: Seamus is present in name only. No active characterization is lost here beyond general background presence; confidence on this entry is low and impact is negligible.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 – Great Hall / Seamus tries to turn water into rum
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book establishes Seamus as someone who talked extensively about flying from childhood ('the way Seamus Finnigan told it, he'd spent most of his childhood zooming around the countryside on his broomstick') and who in Charms got so impatient he prodded the feather with his wand and set it on fire. His defining comic trait is impulsive, over-eager magic that backfires. The book does not include a scene of him attempting to turn water into rum.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film invents a scene where Seamus attempts to turn a cup of water into rum ('Eye of rabbit, harp string hum...'), which results in an explosion that chars him. This is actually consistent with his book trait of impulsive magic going wrong. The invented spell-attempt is a net-faithful extrapolation.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is largely faithful in spirit – the film translates his book trait of reckless, backfiring magic into a new invented gag. Minor damage only arises from the fact that the specific flavour (trying to make alcohol) gives him a slightly different, more roguish characterization than the book supports, but the corpus does not contradict it strongly enough to score this as significant damage.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 – Charms class / Wingardium Leviosa, Seamus's feather explosion
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book explicitly states: 'Seamus got so impatient that he prodded it with his wand and set fire to it -- Harry had to put it out with his hat.' Seamus's failure is impulsive impatience; Harry actively helps him by putting the fire out. This is a small moment of peer interaction and Seamus's characterization.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film shows Seamus causing an explosion with his feather (shown twice – Scenes 4 and 5), consistent with his impulsive trait. However, Harry's act of putting out the fire with his hat – a small but humanizing peer-interaction beat – is absent. The film version is purely Seamus failing alone, with no Harry involvement.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The loss of Harry extinguishing Seamus's fire with his hat removes a small moment of casual Gryffindor dormitory camaraderie between them. The damage is minor but real: it slightly flattens their easy peer dynamic.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 – Seamus's self-introduction at the feast
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Seamus's half-and-half parentage revelation ('Me dad's a Muggle. Mom didn't tell him she was a witch 'til after they were married. Bit of a nasty shock for him.') is offered as part of a group conversation about families, with 'the others laughed' indicating he's a socially easy, warm presence in the group.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film reproduces the line closely ('I'm half and half. Me dad's a Muggle. Mam's a witch. Bit of a nasty shock for him when he found out.') but it is delivered to Harry alone, somewhat out of context from the group family discussion. The communal warmth and group laughter of the book moment is absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The line itself is faithfully reproduced, but the social context – a relaxed group exchange that shows Seamus as a naturally funny, warmly received member of the Gryffindor peer group – is slightly reduced. Damage is minor.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 (Lockhart's classroom / Cornish pixies) — Seamus identified by name as the one who laughs
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scenes 12-15 establish Seamus as the student who cannot control his laughter at the pixies, then chokes out a skeptical question ('Well, they're not — they're not very — dangerous, are they?'), showing his irreverent wit and confident willingness to mock Lockhart directly to his face.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film preserves Seamus's laugh and his identification ('Cornish pixies?') and Lockhart's retort ('Laugh if you will, Mr. Finnegan'), but gives Seamus no spoken follow-up challenge or choked skeptical question. His moment is reduced to a single reactive snort before the chaos erupts, losing his voice and the beat where he presses the point.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book gives Seamus a two-beat comic exchange — the laugh and then the sardonic follow-up question — that characterises him as someone who not only finds Lockhart ridiculous but says so. The film keeps only the laugh, trimming his personality to a reaction rather than an active comic voice. Damage is minor and isolated.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 (Lockhart's classroom) — Seamus absent from pixie chaos aftermath
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scene 29 places Seamus in the duelling-club aftermath being held up by Ron after Ron's broken wand does something to him ('Ron was holding up an ashen-faced Seamus, apologizing for whatever his broken wand had done'). This establishes a small but concrete moment of physical comedy and peer bond between Ron and Seamus.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film's pixie chaos and its aftermath (scenes 2 and the corridor scene 42B) show only Harry, Ron, Hermione, and Neville dealing with consequences. Seamus is absent from any named interaction in the aftermath; the Ron-holding-up-Seamus beat is entirely absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: A small but characterising moment of Ron-Seamus camaraderie and Seamus's participation in the comic chaos is lost. Seamus is reduced to a background figure rather than an active participant with a named peer relationship. Damage is minor.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 (Duelling Club, Great Hall scene 70) — Seamus's fear reaction after Parseltongue incident
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book does not show Seamus at the duelling club itself in the provided corpus, but film corpus scene 70/71 is the relevant evidence. The film corpus (scene 71) explicitly states: 'Even Seamus, Neville, and Dean Thomas walk by without a word' after Harry's Parseltongue incident, depicting Seamus as part of the fearful, ostracising crowd.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film corpus (scene 71) shows Seamus, Neville, and Dean walking by Harry without a word, treating him with suspicion and fear. The book corpus (scene 6, 9, 12-15, 35) consistently portrays Seamus as irreverent, laughing, and unafraid — someone who mocks authority and finds danger funny rather than recoiling from a classmate.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Seamus's book characterisation is one of irreverence and confidence; he laughs at Lockhart, mocks danger, and pretends to vomit at Snape's sycophancy. The film uses him as part of the generic fearful-crowd reaction to Harry's Parseltongue, which flattens his personality into generic peer pressure and timidity. This is a trait alteration: the confident, sardonic Seamus becomes an undifferentiated frightened classmate.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 (Common Room, scene 108) — Seamus's line about Hogwarts closing
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scene 37 gives Seamus the howled line 'Exams? We're still getting exams?' — a comic, self-centred outburst that captures his personality perfectly: irreverent, funny, prioritising his own comfort even in crisis. Book scene 20 gives him an intellectually engaged question to Binns about the Chamber. These establish Seamus as vocally comic and genuinely curious.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film scene 108 (Common Room after McGonagall's announcement) gives Seamus the line 'They can't close Hogwarts. Where would we all go?' This is a straight, mildly anxious reaction line with no comic irreverence. It replaces his book voice (mock-outrage about exams, sardonic wit) with a generic worried-student line.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film gives Seamus a line in this scene, which is positive, but the line does not reflect his book characterisation at all. His book voice is irreverent and self-deprecatingly comic ('Exams? We're still getting exams?'). The film line is generic worried exposition. The substitution slightly misrepresents who Seamus is, though the damage is limited given the brevity of both moments.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film corpus overall — absence of Seamus's Chamber-of-Secrets question to Binns
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scene 20 gives Seamus an engaged, substantive question in History of Magic: 'if the Chamber can only be opened by Slytherin's true heir, no one else would be able to find it, would they?' This shows intellectual curiosity about the central mystery and active participation in a key world-building scene.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film corpus contains no History of Magic class scene and no equivalent moment of Seamus engaging intellectually with the Chamber mystery. The scene is replaced by Hermione asking McGonagall about the Chamber in Transfiguration (film scene 2, scene 62). Seamus's intellectual participation in establishing the mystery is entirely absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The transfer of the Chamber-lore scene from Binns's class (where Seamus participates) to McGonagall's class (where Hermione leads) is a broader structural change, but it incidentally removes a moment where Seamus demonstrates active engagement with the plot's central mystery. The loss is minor for Seamus specifically but contributes to his overall reduction to comic/reactive background figure.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film corpus overall — absence of Seamus pretending to vomit into his cauldron (Snape scene)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scene 35 shows Seamus pretending to vomit into his cauldron as Malfoy flatters Snape — a small but vivid piece of silent physical comedy that underscores his irreverence toward authority and his alignment with the Gryffindor perspective on Slytherin sycophancy.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: No equivalent moment appears in the film corpus. The Potions dungeon scenes in the film corpus do not include this beat.
damaging_scenes.explanation: A small characterising moment of Seamus's physical comedy and anti-authority irreverence is absent. Individually minor, but it is part of a pattern across the film of Seamus losing his distinct comic personality and becoming a background Gryffindor.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 (Divination class) — Seamus mishears 'Grim' as 'Grin'
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book corpus (Scenes 4–6), Seamus participates in the tea-leaf reading with casual skepticism, tilting his head, making light observations ('it looks like a Grim if you do this... but it looks more like a donkey from here'), and showing irreverent humor without being made to look foolish or dim.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film has Seamus ask 'The Grin? What's the Grin?' — a malapropism that makes him appear slow or inattentive, prompting Parvati to correct him with 'Not the grin, you idiot.' This reframes his humor as accidental buffoonery rather than the knowing, light skepticism the books establish.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book Seamus is casually witty and observant in this scene; the film reduces him to a comic dunce who misunderstands a basic word. The 'idiot' label from Parvati reinforces this reframing. It's a small but clear shift in how his intelligence and humor register to the audience.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 (Boggart lesson) — Seamus correctly identifies the Boggart unprompted
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book corpus (Scenes 12–20) shows Seamus as apprehensive ('eyed the now rattling doorknob apprehensively') but then courageous and successful in the lesson, dispatching the banshee and celebrating afterward. His knowledge is shown through action, not exposition.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film gives Seamus the line 'That's a Boggart, that is' in a hushed voice, which Lupin praises with 'Very good, Mr. Finnigan.' This is a minor faithful beat in isolation, but coming immediately after the 'Grin/Grim' exchange where he appeared dim, it creates an inconsistent characterization — he seems to randomly know things rather than having a coherent personality.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This beat is not inherently damaging, but in context it compounds the inconsistency introduced by the 'Grin' moment. The corpus does not show Seamus's apprehension before the wardrobe (book Scene 13), which is replaced by this expository identification. Minor on its own; noted for cumulative effect.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 5 (Sir Cadogan portrait) — Seamus's complaint reduced to a single dismissive line
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 29 shows Seamus directing his frustration at Percy, a more senior student, with a direct complaint: 'He's a complete lunatic. Can't we get anyone else?' This shows social confidence — Seamus will address authority figures directly when annoyed.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film retains 'He's barking mad!' but strips the social dimension entirely. There is no address to an authority figure; it is just a throwaway exclamation into the air. The line itself is consistent in sentiment but loses the characterization of Seamus confidently voicing grievances upward.
damaging_scenes.explanation: A small but real loss. The book moment shows Seamus has social assertiveness; the film version is just ambient grumbling. The change is minor but contributes to a pattern of thinning his personality to reactive one-liners.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 6 (Firebolt reveal) — Seamus's celebration line is a request, not a cheer
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 38 has Seamus give a full-throated cheer: 'Good for you, Harry!' — an expression of genuine enthusiasm and warmth toward Harry, consistent with their friendly dormitory relationship established across multiple book scenes.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film replaces this with 'Can I have a go, Harry? After you, of course —' which reframes Seamus's reaction as self-interested excitement about the broom rather than warm support for Harry. The social dynamic shifts from camaraderie to opportunism.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book line affirms the friendly Gryffindor bond between Seamus and Harry. The film line, while not hostile, redirects Seamus's motivation toward personal desire for the broom. It subtly erodes the sense of genuine friendship and replaces warmth with comic self-interest, which is a mild but real relationship-level shift.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 7 (Firebolt test outside) — Seamus encourages Harry with 'Go on, Harry'
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: No direct book equivalent in the corpus for this outdoor test scene, but the book corpus consistently shows Seamus as an enthusiastic and warm dormitory companion who cheers Harry's successes (Scene 38).
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Seamus says 'Go on, Harry' — a brief, encouraging line that is broadly consistent with his book characterization as a supportive Gryffindor peer.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is essentially faithful. No meaningful damage. Included only to note that it is the one film moment that aligns with book Seamus's warmth toward Harry. It slightly offsets the damage from Scene 6 but does not undo the pattern of reduction.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 – Great Hall, Beauxbatons arrival: Seamus comments on Madame Maxime
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book establishes Seamus as a lively, gregarious Gryffindor who makes snarky, opinionated comments about people and events (e.g., contemptuously dismissing Diggory, making jokes with Dean). His humor is confident and socially engaged.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Seamus's one line is 'Blimey. That's one big woman.' – a reductive, laddish remark that reduces his characterization to a single crude observation, stripping away his more layered commentary and social personality.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor but symptomatic: Seamus is given a single throwaway line that flattens his voice. In the books he offers more textured opinions (e.g., his contemptuous dismissal of Diggory, his enthusiastic Ireland pride). The film's only real characterization beat for him here is a crude size joke, reducing him to comic relief rather than a rounded peer.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 – Defense Against the Dark Arts classroom: Seamus's whispered comment about Moody
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book establishes Seamus as someone who reacts vocally and expressively to lessons and events – revolted by bubotuber pus, sniggering at Ron and Harry's Trelawney impressions, asking what the egg screech was. He participates actively in classroom life as a peer voice.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Seamus whispers 'No way. The old codger can see out the back of his head.' – a very brief background comment. While present, this is his only classroom beat and it is whispered rather than openly voiced, diminishing his established pattern of confident, out-loud classroom reactions.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor reduction in Seamus's established vocal confidence in classroom settings. The books give him multiple moments of open, uninhibited commentary; the film reduces this to a single hushed aside.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 – Campsite/World Cup: Seamus entirely absent from the Ireland/campsite scenes
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scenes 2–6 establish Seamus at the World Cup with his mother and Dean, proudly displaying Irish colors, engaging Harry, Ron, and Hermione warmly, still wearing his Ireland rosette afterward. This is a key moment of Seamus's Irish identity, his relationship with his mother, and his social bond with Harry's group.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Seamus does not appear in the campsite scenes at all. Mrs. Finnigan and the shamrock tent are absent. There is no Ireland rosette, no national pride moment, and no family context for Seamus whatsoever.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The World Cup campsite is the only moment in the book corpus where Seamus's Irish identity, his home life (his mother), and his enthusiastic personality are shown together. Losing this removes the only characterization that distinguishes him from a generic background Gryffindor. His continuing to wear the rosette afterward (book scene 6, 10) reinforces personality continuity that simply does not exist in the film.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 – Grounds/Potter Stinks badge scene: Seamus walking with Ron, passive
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scene 34 shows Ron standing with Dean and Seamus during the badge incident, not sticking up for Harry – a meaningful moment of social pressure and fractured friendship that implicates Seamus in the peer dynamic. Seamus is a named presence in a morally charged moment.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film shows Ron and Seamus walking together (Seamus is visible), but Seamus has no reaction or line. He is a background body rather than a participant in the social fracture being dramatized.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Small loss: Seamus's complicit passivity in the book (present but not defending Harry) is a minor but real character note. The film makes him invisible in the same beat, losing even that minimal characterization.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 – Seamus's line about blowing things up
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book corpus does not establish Seamus's tendency to accidentally blow things up (this is primarily a books 1–3 running gag not evidenced in the provided book corpus for GoF). In the GoF book corpus, Seamus is characterized by his opinions, humor, Ireland pride, and social energy – not by accidental explosions.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Seamus says 'It's not like l try to blow things up, exactly. It just happens a fair bit. You have to admit, though, fire's pretty fascinating.' This reduces his entire personality to a single slapstick trait – the hapless pyromaniac – which is not the characterization present in the GoF book corpus.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is Seamus's most substantial speaking moment in the film, and it defines him purely by a comedic accident-prone trait rather than the confident, opinionated, socially engaged character of the book corpus. While the explosion gag exists in the wider book series, using it as his sole defining line in this film flattens him into a one-note comic device, actively replacing his richer GoF characterization.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 – Yule Ball preparation: Seamus present but wordless
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scene 58–61 has Harry, Ron, Seamus, Dean, and Neville getting ready together, with Seamus going to the ball with Lavender (book scene 50) – a small but social moment. Seamus is embedded in the male dormitory group dynamic leading up to the ball.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film shows Ron and Harry preparing; the dormitory group scene is compressed and Seamus has no lines or individual presence. His date with Lavender is unmentioned.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor loss of group social texture. Seamus's participation in the Yule Ball preparations and his date with Lavender are cut, removing a small piece of his social life and personality.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 – Transfiguration/dance lesson: Ron whispers to Seamus
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Books portray Seamus as an active, vocal participant in social and classroom moments, openly commenting and sniggering rather than being whispered at.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Ron whispers something to Seamus during McGonagall's dance lesson, and Seamus laughs. Seamus is purely a passive audience for Ron's joke rather than an initiator or co-creator of humor.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Small but consistent pattern: in the film, Seamus is repeatedly the recipient of other characters' humor rather than a generator of it, inverting his book personality where he is frequently the one making the snarky remark.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 5 – Second task poolside: Seamus asks 'What's the matter with him?' and tells Dean to get Harry a towel
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book corpus, Seamus is a supportive, enthusiastic friend who cheers Harry on (waving and sniggering at the Yule Ball, asking about the egg, celebrating with the group). His relationship with Harry is warm peer camaraderie.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Seamus has two brief functional lines: 'What's the matter with him?' (confused by Harry choking on gillyweed) and 'Go get him another towel' (after the task). These are purely practical, logistical lines with no warmth or personality.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Seamus's lines in the second task sequence reduce him to a concerned bystander giving stage directions rather than a character with a voice. The book's version of Seamus would have a more colorful reaction.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 6 – After second task: 'Well done!' from Seamus
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book establishes Seamus as expressive and opinionated in group celebrations and reactions (the Goblet of Fire night, the egg scene in the common room where he asks what the clue is).
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Seamus's only contribution to Harry's second-task success is a brief 'Well done!' in the crowd, indistinguishable from any background character.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Consistent with the film's overall treatment: Seamus is reduced to generic crowd reaction rather than a named, characterized peer. Minimal individual damage on its own but part of a sustained pattern.

damaging_scenes.scene: Order of the Phoenix – dormitory confrontation (film scene 1)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the books, Seamus's opening position is carefully shaded: he avoids Harry's eye, turns his back, speaks 'in a measured voice', and only reveals his mother's view reluctantly and with evident discomfort. He is not openly aggressive until Harry insults his mother. His question about Cedric ('what did happen that night...?') is asked 'sounding nervous and eager at the same time', showing genuine curiosity beneath the hostility. The conflict is a slow, painful escalation rooted in Seamus's genuine divided loyalty between family and friend.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film collapses the slow, awkward build into a brisk exchange. Seamus's first line is direct and unguarded: 'Let me see, uh, because of you. The Daily Prophet's been saying a lot of things about you, Harry, and about Dumbledore as well.' There is no physical avoidance, no measured discomfort, no nervous curiosity about Cedric. The nuanced emotional texture – divided loyalty, embarrassment, reluctance – is replaced with a blunt statement of position.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book uses Seamus's body language and hesitancy to establish that he is not a villain but a boy caught between his mother and his friend. Flattening this into a direct statement removes the sympathetic internal conflict that makes Seamus a meaningful representative of the wider wizarding public's doubt, reducing him to a simple antagonist for the scene.

damaging_scenes.scene: Order of the Phoenix – dormitory confrontation, Harry's insult (film scene 1)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Harry insults Seamus's mother only after Seamus has delivered the most wounding line ('Yeah, something like that' confirming his mother thinks Harry is a liar). Harry's anger is a reaction to sustained provocation. The escalation follows a clear emotional logic: Harry is already 'sick of it' and finally snaps.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film, Harry says 'I guess you should read the Prophet then, like your stupid mother' almost immediately after Seamus raises his mother's doubts. The provocation Harry has received at that point is much lighter, making Harry's insult feel disproportionately aggressive and less sympathetic.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book carefully justifies Harry's anger so the audience understands rather than judges him. By triggering Harry's outburst earlier in the exchange, the film makes Harry look more needlessly cruel, subtly damaging his characterisation and reducing the audience's ability to fully side with him in the dispute.

damaging_scenes.scene: Order of the Phoenix – Seamus's question about Cedric absent from film (film scene 1)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: After the initial flare-up cools slightly, book-Seamus asks, 'what did happen that night when... with Cedric Diggory and all?' sounding 'nervous and eager at the same time'. This beat is crucial: it shows that beneath his publicly declared scepticism Seamus genuinely wants to know the truth, that he is capable of curiosity and ambivalence, and it foreshadows his eventual reconciliation with Harry.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film omits this question entirely. The confrontation moves straight from insult to shouting match without Seamus showing any crack of genuine curiosity or openness.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The question humanises Seamus and plants the seed for his later apology. Without it, his eventual reconciliation (film scene 2) feels more abrupt and less earned, and the portrait of him as a boy genuinely torn by doubt rather than simply hostile is lost.

damaging_scenes.scene: Order of the Phoenix – Neville's defence of Harry cut (excluded theatrical material)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Neville's 'We believe Harry. My gran's always said You-Know-Who would come back one day...' speech directly follows Seamus's contemptuous exit and acts as a counterpoint to it. It also triggers Harry's 'rush of gratitude towards Neville' and closes the scene with Seamus isolated in his position rather than validated.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This scene was cut from the theatrical release. The dormitory scene ends without Neville's defence, removing the moral counterweight to Seamus's hostility within the dormitory group dynamic.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Without Neville's rebuttal, the dormitory scene ends on Seamus's contempt with no in-group correction. The book uses this beat to show that Seamus is the outlier, not Harry, which is important to the audience's understanding of how isolated Harry's doubters really are among his closest peers. Its absence weakens the scene's resolution and the Seamus–Harry dynamic's context.

damaging_scenes.scene: Order of the Phoenix – Seamus's reconciliation (film scene 2)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Seamus's reconciliation is a quiet, awkward, deeply private moment: 'he mumbled, squinting at Harry's left knee', telling Harry he believes him and has sent a copy of the magazine to his mother. It occurs outside Transfiguration, without an audience, and is characterised by typical teenage difficulty with apology – halting, indirect, physically evasive.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film places Seamus's apology ('I wanted to apologize. Now even me mum says The Prophet's version of things don't add up. So, what I'm really trying to say is that I believe you.') in a context adjacent to a DA meeting, making it more openly stated and less physically awkward. The key element that he has sent the magazine to his mother is absent, removing the detail that shows he has actively worked to change his mother's view.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's reconciliation is characterised by endearing teenage awkwardness and the meaningful detail of the magazine copy. The film's version is cleaner but flatter. The loss of the magazine detail also removes the echo of Seamus's mother, who was the original source of the conflict, leaving the reconciliation slightly less complete.

damaging_scenes.scene: Order of the Phoenix – ongoing dormitory tension (book scenes 41–55) largely absent from film
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The books depict a sustained cold war between Harry and Seamus across multiple scenes: Seamus dressing at top speed and leaving before Harry wakes, Dean being unable to defend Seamus but following him out, Seamus handing back Harry's essay without eye contact, Harry passing Seamus and having 'a fleeting impression that Seamus had opened his mouth to speak'. This drip of social friction over days establishes the psychological toll on Harry.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: After the initial confrontation, the film provides no scenes of the ongoing cold war. There is no depiction of Seamus avoiding Harry in the dormitory or the awkward essay exchange. The tension is simply absent until the apology.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book uses Seamus's sustained coldness to illustrate the cumulative weight of being disbelieved – Harry notes he was 'shaken by the argument with Seamus, whom he had always liked very much' and wonders 'how many more attacks like Seamus's he would have to endure'. Removing this sustained tension reduces the emotional journey from conflict to reconciliation and weakens the portrayal of Harry's social isolation as an ongoing lived experience rather than a single incident.

damaging_scenes.scene: Order of the Phoenix – Seamus's 'confused and defiant' expression after Ernie's vote of confidence absent from film
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: After Ernie Macmillan publicly declares his belief in Harry, the book notes that Harry 'caught Seamus's expression, which looked both confused and defiant.' This is a small but telling beat: Seamus is not simply hostile but is genuinely thrown by public support for Harry, suggesting his scepticism is wavering before the formal apology.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film has no equivalent scene. There is no moment between the initial confrontation and the apology in which Seamus visibly processes his position being challenged.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This beat provides a midpoint on Seamus's arc from doubter to believer, showing the private erosion of his position. Without it, the arc moves in only two beats (confrontation and apology) instead of three, making Seamus's change of heart slightly less psychologically textured.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 (Quidditch tryouts montage) - Seamus sends Bludger into stands
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book establishes Seamus as a Chaser candidate who is outflown by Dean at tryouts (HBP ch.11), and as a roommate who participates in normal dormitory life, banter, and social dynamics. He is not portrayed as incompetent or comedically dangerous.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Seamus is shown as a Beater at tryouts, sending a Bludger rocketing into the stands and scattering onlookers — played purely for slapstick comedy. This repositions him as comic relief defined by dangerous incompetence rather than a credible Chaser contestant.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Seamus loses the Chaser spot to Dean on merit after a genuine competition. The film replaces his legitimate athletic arc with a throwaway gag that reduces him to bumbling comic relief, altering his characterization from a plausible athlete to a figure of mockery.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 (Great Hall morning of Quidditch match) - Seamus tells Ron he has two Galleons on Gryffindor
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book does not frame Seamus as someone who gambles on Quidditch matches or whose primary function in a scene is to add social pressure to Ron before a game. His interactions with Harry and Ron are casual dormitory-level friendship without a defined 'pressure' role.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Seamus appears briefly solely to tell Ron he has two Galleons riding on Gryffindor, adding external pressure and then immediately exiting. He functions as a minor plot device to heighten Ron's anxiety rather than as a character with his own voice or presence.
damaging_scenes.explanation: While minor, this reduces Seamus to a single-line functional cameo whose sole purpose is to service Ron's storyline. Combined with the slapstick Bludger gag, it establishes a pattern of Seamus existing only as a background utility figure rather than a peer with his own characterization.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 (Corridor - Seamus in alcove laughing with Dean while Ginny sits by) - background positioning
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book (HBP ch.24) establishes tension between Dean and Seamus and Harry over Quidditch team selection, and Seamus's relationship with Dean is that of close friends and dormitory roommates with genuine camaraderie and shared reactions (e.g., both roar with laughter at Ron's levitation). Seamus also has his own distinct moments of curiosity and dialogue (e.g., the Inferius/ghost question to Snape, the Apparition enthusiasm).
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Seamus appears wordlessly in the background laughing with Dean while Ginny sits apart looking toward Harry. He exists purely as set dressing to frame the Ginny-Harry visual beat, with no independent characterization.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Seamus is used as a background prop to visually isolate Ginny for a Harry/Ginny beat. While individually small, this is symptomatic of the film's consistent reduction of Seamus to a backgrounded, functionless presence, compounding the overall flattening of his character.

damaging_scenes.scene: Deathly Hallows Part 2 - Room of Requirement arrival / DA reunion
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Seamus actively explains the Room of Requirement's defences to Harry, Ron and Hermione with enthusiasm and authority: 'It's a proper hideout, as long as one of us stays in here, they can't get at us... You've just got to make sure you close the loopholes. Neville's the man!' He also asks eager, engaged questions ('What were you after?', 'What's the plan?') and delivers the wry realist line 'That's nothing to go on.' He is a participant with voice and standing in the group.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film, Seamus's first line on arrival is a throwaway joke at Aberforth's expense ('Not more of Aberforth's cooking, I hope. Be a surprise if we could digest it.') and his second contribution is the single line 'That's nothing to go on.' The entire explanation of the Room's defensive properties — his clearest moment of competent, knowledgeable speech in the book — is cut. His role is reduced to comic relief and a single sceptical quip.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book uses this scene to establish Seamus as a resilient, informed survivor who understands the Room and actively contributes information. The film strips that competence away, leaving only comedy. His character voice is flattened at the first meaningful opportunity.

damaging_scenes.scene: Deathly Hallows Part 2 - Room of Requirement: Seamus describes two weeks in hiding
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book gives Seamus an extended speech describing life in the Room over nearly two weeks: makeshift hammocks, the bathroom that appeared when girls arrived, the general texture of DA resistance life. This grounds him as a long-term participant in the resistance, not a latecomer, and gives him narrative real estate.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This speech is entirely absent from the film corpus. The film provides no equivalent account of the DA's experience hiding in the Room. Seamus is present as a background figure but delivers no such testimony.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Removing this speech costs Seamus his primary moment of narrative weight in the book's Hogwarts section. It also erases the audience's understanding of what the DA endured before Harry's return, and Seamus's specific place in that story.

damaging_scenes.scene: Deathly Hallows Part 2 - Dean's return / Seamus's reunion hug
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book gives Seamus a brief but emotionally significant beat: 'Seamus gave a great roar of delight and ran to hug his best friend' when Dean arrives. This is the only direct expression of the Seamus–Dean friendship in the entire book corpus, and it is vivid and characterful.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film corpus, Dean Thomas is listed as already present in the Room of Requirement when Harry arrives (Film Scene 4 notes 'Dean Thomas' among the faces). There is no equivalent reunion moment between Seamus and Dean, and no expression of their friendship.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The Seamus–Dean friendship is one of the few defined interpersonal bonds Seamus has in the books. Its sole expressive moment in this portion of the narrative is lost entirely, leaving their relationship invisible on screen.

damaging_scenes.scene: Deathly Hallows Part 2 - Seamus casting a Patronus to repel Dementors
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book explicitly places Seamus among three DA members — Luna, Ernie, and Seamus — who arrive in the nick of time to cast Patronuses alongside Harry, Ron, and Hermione when their own Patronuses are failing. Seamus casts a silver fox Patronus. Ron then directly thanks Luna, Ernie, and Seamus. This is a clear moment of courage, magical competence, and active rescue.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This entire sequence — the Dementor attack, the failing Patronuses, and Seamus's timely arrival to help — does not appear in the film corpus. There is no corresponding scene.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is Seamus's single most significant act of agency in the book's battle sequence. He actively saves Harry, Ron, and Hermione. Its complete absence removes his only heroic set-piece in the Battle of Hogwarts, reducing him to a background combatant with no individual moment of courage or magical achievement during the battle proper.

damaging_scenes.scene: Deathly Hallows Part 2 - Neville's speech to Voldemort / 'Stand down, Neville!'
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book there is no equivalent scene where Seamus angrily tells Neville to stand down. In the book's equivalent moment, Neville acts autonomously and the crowd's reaction is not characterised by Seamus opposing him.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film (Scene 13), when Neville begins his speech to Voldemort, Seamus shouts 'Stand down, Neville!' angrily and tries to physically push forward, only stopped by Ron gripping his arm. This presents Seamus as someone who would capitulate or prevent defiance at the story's most critical moment of collective courage.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film invents a moment of cowardice or defeatism for Seamus at the saga's climactic turning point. In the books he is a Gryffindor fighter who casts Patronuses to save Harry; here he is the voice urging surrender. This actively contradicts his established characterisation and damages his integrity at the worst possible narrative moment.

damaging_scenes.scene: Deathly Hallows Part 2 - Bridge demolition scenes [CUT - treated as absent]
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book does not contain a bridge demolition sequence, so there is no book baseline being violated. However, the film screenplay contained scenes (235B, 242, 247, 271) in which Seamus is given substantial characterisation — competence, pyrotechnic expertise endorsed by McGonagall, wit, camaraderie with Neville — that constitutes the film's primary attempt to give him individual agency during the battle.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: These scenes were cut from the theatrical release and are excluded from scoring per the non-theatrical material rules. Consequently, the film as released contains no scene in which McGonagall singles out Seamus for a specific task, no scene of him exercising expertise, and no extended comedic-heroic beat with Neville. The only residual trace in the theatrical cut is Trelawney's line 'There's more to me than incense and tea leaves, Mr. Finnegan' (Scenes 11 and 14), which is now contextless.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The cut of the bridge sequence eliminates what was, in the screenplay, the film's compensatory mechanism for Seamus's reduced role — his one extended scene of individual heroic function. Its removal leaves a gap: McGonagall's reference to his 'proclivity for pyrotechnics' and Trelawney's line addressing him are orphaned in the theatrical cut, gesturing at characterisation the audience never sees. The book's Patronus scene was already lost; the bridge scene's cut removes the film's own substitute, leaving Seamus with no moment of individual agency in the battle whatsoever.
